title: Reading the four bars
intro: This level takes the bar chart apart. It sets out what each swap actually writes into the activation, works out how wide the error bars are at ninety trials and what an overlap of that width does and does not establish, and follows the clamp down to what it holds fixed and what it leaves unmeasured.

chapters.title: What each swap writes into the activation
chapters.body:
The left panel of [[fig-16]] prints next-token distributions for a single two-hop prompt whose unspoken bridging concept is China. The first column is the clean forward pass. The second is a raw China-for-France [[lens-coordinate-swap]], the intervention the section's earlier experiments used. The third and fourth exchange the [[intermediate-probe]] for China against the probe for the alternative, along one of its two parts.

The method paragraph describes a third probe condition, a swap along the full probe direction. The prose quotes a success rate for the raw swap, for the [[j-space-component]] and for the remainder, and none for the full probe.

Every one of these edits is the same surgery with a different pair of directions ([[eq-lens-swap]]). The two directions become the columns of a matrix $V$. The activation $h$ is read against them by [[pseudoinverse]], $c = V^\dagger h$, rather than by inner product, because the two directions are not orthogonal and an inner product would let each leak into the other's reading. The two entries of $c$ are then exchanged. The difference $V(\sigma(c) - c)$ is added back to $h$.

Whatever the [[residual-stream]] carries outside the plane spanned by those two directions is left alone.

What changes from condition to condition is only which plane that is. In the raw condition the plane is spanned by two [[j-lens-vector]]s, one per vocabulary token. In the J-space condition each direction is the nonnegative combination of $k = 25$ lens vectors that [[gradient-pursuit]] fitted to the probe. In the remainder condition each direction is the probe with that combination subtracted off.

chapters.title: How wide the bars are at ninety trials
chapters.body:
The [[wilson-interval]] is obtained by inverting the score test for a proportion, not by adding a multiple of the estimated standard error to the observed rate. The simpler Wald interval is the one that misbehaves at the ends of the scale. Near zero or one it can extend past the scale entirely, and its true coverage drops below the nominal 95 percent. Wilson intervals stay inside the scale and are pulled slightly toward one half.

Their width at ninety trials is what settles the comparison. At a rate of $0.61$ the binomial standard error is $\sqrt{0.61 \times 0.39 / 90}$, which comes to about $0.051$. Multiplied by $1.96$ that is roughly $0.10$. The bar therefore spans something close to 51 to 71 percent.

A rate of 60 percent sits near the middle of that span.

What an overlap of this kind establishes is narrow. It shows that ninety trials cannot separate the two rates. It does not show that the rates are equal, and an interval this wide would equally fail to separate 61 percent from the low fifties.

The comparison is still internally clean. The 60 percent for the raw [[jacobian-lens]] swap is a fresh measurement of the [[swap-success-rate]] on the same ninety prompts, taken alongside the component swaps. The 70 percent reported in [[fig-15]] belongs to a different and smaller set. Within one figure every condition faces the same items, which is what the claim about [[internal-reasoning]] in the [[j-space]] requires.

chapters.title: The gap ninety trials can resolve
chapters.body:
The same arithmetic on the remainder's 28 percent gives $\sqrt{0.28 \times 0.72 / 90} \approx 0.047$, and $1.96$ times that is about $0.09$. The remainder's bar spans roughly 19 to 37 percent.

The lower edge of the J-space bar sits near 51 percent and the upper edge of the remainder's near 37. The two do not meet. This is the difference the sample size can resolve, and it is the one the section rests its conclusion on.

The asymmetry underneath it is the point. [[j-space-component-decomposition]] leaves the J-space part holding roughly 10 to 15 percent of the probe's variance and the remainder holding the rest. The smaller edit flips more answers than the larger one. That is consistent with [[j-space-capacity]], which finds the workspace carrying under 10 percent of activation variance throughout.

Two qualifications belong with the numbers. The section quotes no chance-level rate for these bars, so the 28 percent has to be read against 60 and 61 rather than against zero. And the paper treats the [[non-j-space-residual-effect]] as something requiring an account rather than as noise.

The same ordering appeared once already. In [[j-space-privilege-for-report]] a [[concept-vector]] is split the same way, with a median of 6 to 7 percent of its variance in the J-space part. On the think-of-a-category swap that part drove the target into the top five on 59 percent of trials against 88 percent for the pure lens vectors, while the remainder managed 5 percent. One protocol tests [[verbal-report]] and the other tests internal reasoning, and they agree on which part carries the effect.

chapters.title: What the clamp holds, and what it leaves open
chapters.body:
A clean-pass value is recorded rather than computed. The prompt is first run with no intervention, and the coordinates along the chosen lens directions are stored at every layer and every position. The perturbed pass then has those stored values written back in wherever they would otherwise move ([[activation-clamping]]).

Re-imposing them at every layer is the part that does the work. A single edit at one depth can be overwritten by the layers above it. Holding the clean values throughout means no later layer can rebuild the intermediate in those coordinates.

The control clamps the complement of whatever is being swapped ([[complement-clamped-swap-control]]). In the remainder condition the remainder moves while the J-space coordinates stay pinned. Any effect that survives has to travel by some route that does not pass through them. The rate falls from 28 percent to 6.

Six percent is not zero, and the paper offers no account of the residue.

The same control in the report experiments ([[j-space-mediation-clamp]]) drove the remainder's 5 percent top-five rate to zero under the swap protocol, and nearly to zero under concept injection. Three protocols, one direction of result.

Two things the section leaves open. The clamp is a standing intervention held across the whole network, not only the [[workspace-layers]] where the J-space is occupied, and no separate measurement of what clamping alone costs on these ninety prompts is reported. And the figure carries hatched bars for both component swaps while the prose quotes only the remainder's, so what the J-space swap does with the remainder pinned is in the picture and not in the text.

The wholesale version of shutting the workspace is [[j-space-ablation]]. The read and write operations the clamp is assembled from are collected under [[j-lens-interventions]].
